# Practicing

You finished the project. The notebook runs from a clean start, the README says
where the data came from, and Chapter 26 put a link on it. That was Sunday.
It's Tuesday now, you have an hour, and nobody has assigned you anything. What
goes in the hour?

## Three ways to keep going, ordered by what they're worth

Reproducing a published figure is worth more of the hour than the other two
together, and it takes most of this chapter.

### Reproduce one figure from a paper that published its data

A hiring manager wrote this on r/bioinformatics, about filling one near
entry-level job: "I just interviewed over 60 people with PhDs most of whom were
unemployed... Yet nobody ever was like hey look 'I reproduced the results of
these 5-10 papers myself and put the code in my GitHub'. To me this seems like
the most obvious lowest hanging fruit?"

<!-- nlr-allow: 60 -->

Everybody applying can name the tools. Very few arrive with evidence that they
ran somebody else's analysis end to end and can say where it came apart. You
don't need a lab to get that evidence. The data is already public, and the
paper already told you what the answer should be.

The loop has four steps.

1. Pick a paper that deposited its data. Chapter 23 covered where to look, and
   the test is one line long: does the paper name an accession you can fetch?
2. Pick one panel. Not the paper, not the figure. One panel.
3. Rebuild that panel from the deposited data.
4. List every number that came out different, and put the reason next to it.

That list is your *difference log*, and it's the education. It's also the step
I'd bet you drop, because by step 4 the panel already looks finished. Your
numbers will differ from the paper's for reasons that have names, and the names
are dull. A count filter at 5 CPM on their side and 1 on yours. An annotation
release that renamed a gene between their run and your run. Each one you chase
down is a piece of the pipeline you know afterwards and didn't know before.

An answer on Biostars in 2015 called duplicating a published analysis "an
endless stream of WTFs for you to resolve". Nothing cheaper finds the things
you believe that aren't true.

Be honest in the README about what you proved. Reproducing a figure shows you
can run the pipeline and read the data. It doesn't show the finding is correct,
and it doesn't make you a co-author.

### Rosalind and Kaggle, and what each one leaves out

`rosalind.info` is a set of programming problems built on biology, and its FAQ
says it's free and open to the public. Every problem ships a sample dataset
with the output that dataset should give. A problem hands you the data, tells
you the format, and guarantees an answer exists, and real data does none of
those three things. Use it to get fluent at the code, then go back to the
papers.

`kaggle.com` runs prediction competitions, and its own setup documentation says
what one has to contain. There's a dataset. There's an answer key the
organizers hold back. And there's a single metric, chosen before anybody
enters, that scores every submission against that key. Go there if you want to
get fast at handling tables.

::: {.asof}
Rosalind's FAQ and a problem page, and Kaggle's competition documentation, were
checked on 2 August 2026. Names and layouts move; what a problem page and a
competition have to contain doesn't.
:::

The caveat is that same list. Somebody chose the question, picked the
measurement, cleaned the columns and put the answer in one of them. Every one
of those decisions is the work you're trying to learn how to do. A competition
dataset is the last tenth of a real project, delivered with the first nine
tenths already finished by somebody you'll never meet.

::: {.trap}
A tutorial that runs cleanly is telling you about the tutorial. Guided
exercises get built so that the commands work, so a hundred finished exercises
hand you a number for your own ability that somebody else's testing decided in
advance. The number is too high and nothing on the page says so. Then a real
file gives you nothing back, and that reads as a verdict about you instead of a
fact about the file. Spend part of every week on data nobody cleaned for you.
:::

## Two right answers for the same fold change

You already have the file from Part 4, and `Brca1` is Entrez ID 12189 inside
it. This cell asks how far `Brca1` moves in basal cells between virgin and
lactating mice, and it answers twice, by two routes that are both standard.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

counts = pd.read_csv("data/GSE60450_counts.tsv.gz", sep="\t")
samples = pd.read_csv("data/GSE60450_samples.csv")
counts.columns = [c.split("_")[0] for c in counts.columns]
matrix = counts.set_index("EntrezGeneID").drop(columns="Length")
cpm = matrix / matrix.sum() * 1e6

brca1 = cpm.loc[12189]
basal = samples[samples["cell_type"] == "basal"]
virgin = brca1[basal[basal["stage"] == "virgin"]["sample"]]
lactating = brca1[basal[basal["stage"] == "lactating"]["sample"]]

logfc = np.log2(virgin + 1).mean() - np.log2(lactating + 1).mean()
print("basal virgin, mean CPM   ", round(virgin.mean(), 1))
print("basal lactating, mean CPM", round(lactating.mean(), 1))
print("ratio of those two means ", round(virgin.mean() / lactating.mean(), 1))
print("log2 fold change         ", round(logfc, 2))
print("the same, as a ratio     ", round(2 ** logfc, 1))
```

Three numbers describe one change. Divide the two means as printed: 8.3 over
0.9 is 9.2. Divide them before they were rounded, which the third line does,
and you get 9.4. Take the log2 fold change back to a ratio and you get 4.9.

Nothing here is broken. The first two differ because I rounded before dividing,
which earns a line in the log and nothing more. The log route adds 1 to every
value first, so a gene sitting at zero doesn't produce infinity. Adding 1 to
8.3 barely moves it. Adding 1 to 0.9 more than doubles it, and the number that
doubled is the denominator.

So the correction lands almost entirely on the smaller group, and that's the
whole distance between 9.4 and 4.9. Look at the raw counts underneath those
means. The two virgin samples hold 163 reads and 210. The two lactating samples
hold 20 and 17. Small counts are exactly where two ordinary routes come apart,
and Chapter 25 is about what that does to a p-value.

One more line for the log. Put lactating on top instead and 9.4 becomes 0.1,
and 2.29 becomes -2.29. Nothing on the screen says which order you used.

::: {.check}
Your first two lines should read 8.3 and 0.9. A lactating mean near 19 means
you selected luminal cells rather than basal, which is the Chapter 24 mistake
arriving on schedule. If the ratio prints as 0.1 you have virgin and lactating
the other way round, and you now know what that looks like.
:::

## Ninety days at three hours a week

Thirteen weeks is ninety-one days, near enough to ninety. Thirteen weeks at
three hours each is thirty-nine hours, and that's the entire budget the plan
below gets to spend.

| Weeks | What you do | What you have at the end |
|---|---|---|
| 1 to 2 | Choose the paper and one panel. Copy the accession, the file size and the panel's axis labels into a notebook cell. | A brief: one paper, one panel, one accession. |
| 3 to 5 | Load the data. Reproduce the descriptive numbers the methods section states: how many samples, how many per group, how many rows. | A notebook that loads the file and prints counts you can hold against the paper. |
| 6 to 9 | Rebuild the panel. Stop at the first version with the right axes and the right shape. | Your version of the panel, saved as an image next to the published one. |
| 10 to 11 | Write the difference log. One line per number that came out different, each with a cause or an honest "I don't know". | A numbered list. This is the part worth sending to somebody. |
| 12 to 13 | Publish, the way Chapter 26 did it. Restart and run all, write the README, save the copy to GitHub. | A link you can send. |

You're going to lose two weeks. Put them in the calendar rather than in the
plan, so thirteen weeks of work lands about fifteen weeks out. A plan that only
survives an uninterrupted quarter isn't a plan.

Every row above ends in a file, and that's the reason the rows are shaped like
that. You come back after a gap and open the last file you finished. The gap
costs you the block you were inside when you stopped, never a block you already
closed, and never the whole plan.

Two rules for the return. Reread your last artifact before you run anything.
Then restart and run all before you trust any number on the screen. A notebook
left open for two weeks has an empty runtime sitting under output that still
looks alive. A runtime drops on its own after a stretch with nobody touching
it, which Chapter 4 said out loud.

## Exercises

::: {.exercise num="27.1" time="30 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Write the brief for your replication. One paper, one panel, one accession.
:::
::: {.given}
An open-access paper in a subject you can already read the introduction of.
Chapter 23 named the archives and the four questions that decide whether a
dataset is usable.
:::
::: {.produce}
Four lines: the paper's identifier, which panel of which figure you picked, the
accession the data sits under, and the size of the file you'll download.
:::
::: {.check}
Fill the accession line from the paper alone, inside ten minutes. If you can't,
the paper is the wrong paper. Put it down and pick another one. A paper that
never says where its data lives isn't a replication target, whatever else it
is, and there are more papers than there are Tuesdays.
:::

::: {.answerspace lines="5"}
:::
:::

::: {.exercise num="27.2" time="20 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Run the walkthrough cell again on a second gene and account for what changed.
:::
::: {.given}
Entrez ID 110308 is `Krt5`, the basal marker gene Chapter 24 uses to catch the
mislabeled columns. Same two groups, same file, one identifier changed in the
code. Write your prediction down before you run it: will the two routes agree
more closely than they did for `Brca1`, or less?
:::
::: {.produce}
Two numbers, the ratio of the means and the log2 fold change as a ratio, plus
one sentence naming the cause of the gap between them.
:::
::: {.check}
Your two numbers should agree to one decimal place, where `Brca1` had them
nearly a factor of two apart. If they're still far apart, you changed the
Entrez ID in one place and left it alone in another. The sentence you write
should mention the 1 that gets added before the log, and how much of a CPM in
the thousands that 1 is worth.
:::

::: {.answerbox height="1.8in"}
:::

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="KeyError: 'Krt5'"}
Python is speaking. The matrix is indexed on Entrez IDs and not on symbols, so
`Krt5` is not a label in it. Use `110308`, as an integer and not as text.
Go back to Chapter 20 for why that file holds numbers and not names.
:::

::: {.errfix err="The printed numbers come back as nan"}
No layer is speaking. No traceback, no red text, and the cell finished. Pandas
hands back `nan` for the mean of an empty group, so one of your two groups came
back with no samples in it. The sample table writes `basal`, `virgin` and
`lactating` in lowercase, and `Virgin` matches no row at all. Print each group
and count its rows before you average anything.
:::

::: {.errfix err="FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'data/GSE60450_counts.tsv.gz'"}
Python is speaking, and it's telling you nothing sits at the path you handed
it. A fresh Colab runtime starts with an empty disk, so whatever put the book's
`data` folder into your notebook in Chapter 20 has to run again in this
session, above this cell.
:::

::: {.errfix err="The paper you picked reports a number you cannot get anywhere near"}
Record the gap and go on. A difference you can't explain is still a line in
the log, and "I don't know why this is 2-fold out" is a more useful sentence
than a silent number. Come back to it after the panel is built.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
- Name the four steps of the replication loop, and say which one is the
  education
- Write a difference log entry: the published number, your number, the cause
- State what reproducing a figure proves and what it doesn't
- Say what a competition dataset has already had done to it
- Compute a fold change two ways and explain why the smaller group moves more
- Name the artifact that ends each block of your ninety-day plan
:::
